Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

is it …? phrase

yes-or-no questions

also isn’t it?, are you …?, do you …?, did you …?, have you …?, surely not?, yes-or-no question, does …?, do (in questions)

classical

Plaut. Trin. 50: Valēn'? valuistīn'?
Catull. 9.3: vēnistīne domum ad tuōs penātēs?

-ne

enclitic particle, joined to the first word of the question

(asks a question) is it …? do you …?

The open question, expecting neither yes nor no; it goes on the word asked about, most often the verb (Lewis & Short). In speech it is worn down to -n'. The answer repeats the verb, Valeō (see “yes”); in speech the particle may be left off and the voice alone ask (tū hīc erās?, Ter. Ad. 901).

Other words

  • nōnne — isn’t it? don’t you? (expecting yes)

    adverb, at the head of the question · also used · classical · Plaut. Amph. 406: nōnne ego nunc stō ante aedēs nostrās?; Cic. N. D. 3.89: nōnne animadvertis? (Lewis & Short)

  • num — surely not? (expecting no); whether

    adverb, at the head of the question · also used · classical · Ter. Ph. 846: Num tū intellegis hīc quid narret?; Hor. S. 1.9.6: numquid vīs?

    Numquid vīs?, “anything else?”, is the everyday way of taking leave (Lewis & Short). In an indirect question num is “whether”.

  • an — or …?; (opening a question) so …? can it be that …?

    conjunction · also used · classical · Ter. Hec. 346: Quid ais? an vēnit Pamphilus?

    Introduces the second half of a double question: utrum … an, -ne … an, “is it this or that?” (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • Valēn'? valuistīn'? — Valeō, et valuī rēctius.

    Are you well? Have you been well? — I’m well, and I’ve been better.Plaut. Trin. 50–50b

  • vēnistīne domum ad tuōs penātēs frātrēsque ūnanimōs anumque mātrem?

    have you come home to your own hearth, your loving brothers and your old mother?Catull. 9.3–4

  • Dīc mihi, aufūgistīne? — Era, factum.

    Tell me, did you run away? — Yes, mistress, I did.Ter. Eun. 850

  • Num tū intellegis hīc quid narret? — Num tū? — Nihil. — Tantundem ego.

    You don’t understand what he’s saying, do you? — Do you? — Not a word. — Nor I.Ter. Ph. 846

  • nōnne ego nunc stō ante aedēs nostrās? nōn mī est lanterna in manū?

    Am I not standing in front of our house? Haven’t I a lantern in my hand?Plaut. Amph. 406

  • Quid agitur, Aeschine? — Ehem, pater mī, tū hīc erās?

    How are things, Aeschinus? — Oh, father, you were here?Ter. Ad. 901

See also yes, there is, which, do.
